item.title: Seasons of Wonder Has Arrived
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
As the days grow shorter and the world turns toward winter, we invite you to embrace a season defined not by hibernation, but by discovery.

Our November/December issue, Seasons of Wonder, explores the places, people, and experiences that remind us why we travel: to be surprised, challenged, inspired, and transformed.

In this issue, you’ll discover:

❄️ Finding Sisu
Journey across Finland from Helsinki to the Arctic Circle, where icy plunges, steaming saunas, and the Finnish philosophy of sisu reveal a powerful lesson about courage, resilience, and meeting winter on its own terms.

🌴 Which French Polynesia Are You?
Beyond the postcards lies a collection of islands as varied as the travelers who visit them. From romantic private-island retreats to adventurous cultural explorations, discover which version of paradise speaks to you.

🦁 When the Wild Comes Into View
A celebration of those unforgettable moments when nature stops being scenery and becomes something far more personal.

✨ The Light We Carry Into Winter
Our closing essay reflects on an unexpected evening in Helsinki and the enduring truth that some of travel’s most meaningful moments arrive completely unplanned.

And that’s only the beginning.

From holiday-season Manhattan and the hidden heart of Sweden to culinary storytelling in Carlsbad and conservation-minded luxury in Belize, Seasons of Wonder is filled with journeys designed to inspire your next adventure.

Coming Soon: The print edition of our November/December issue will be arriving on newsstands and available for purchase shortly.

Thank you for traveling with us.

Warm regards,

Sandra Thomas-Comenole
Editor-in-Chief
Curated Travel Magazine

item.title: From Wine Country to the Waterfront
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Tracing the scenic arc from Blue Ridge vineyards to the historic docks of Baltimore.

A driving loop through the Mid-Atlantic offers one of the East Coast’s most compelling geographic pairings: the tranquil, mountain-backed estate roads of Northern Virginia and the vibrant, historic harbor districts of Maryland. Connected by a brief ninety-minute drive across the Potomac, Loudoun County and Baltimore form an effortless country-to-coast circuit.

Start along the winding gravel lanes and scenic stretches of Loudoun County’s Snickersville Turnpike. Tucked beneath the Blue Ridge foothills, historic enclaves like Leesburg, Waterford, and Middleburg offer a slow, equestrian-paced rhythm defined by independent boutiques, farm-to-table dining, and historic hideaways like The Red Fox Inn & Tavern. With over 50 wineries and craft breweries scattered across the hillsides—including hilltop stops like Bluemont Vineyard and Dirt Farm Brewing—the route pairs sweeping valley overlooks with quiet, backroad wandering.

Trading country lanes for city cobblestones, a short eastward drive brings you directly into the maritime heritage of Baltimore. The urban landscape shifts dramatically toward waterfront districts like Fell’s Point and Harbor East, where historic brick rowhouses frame one of the region’s most dynamic food scenes. Here, road-trippers can transition from morning vineyard tours to afternoons eating Maryland crab cakes at Faidley’s or Chesapeake oysters along Thames Street.

Culturally, the city delivers striking depth—from the soaring cast-iron stacks of the George Peabody Library and the eccentric galleries of the American Visionary Art Museum to the National Museum of Railroad History & Innovation, which honors two centuries of American transit legacy.

By combining the open space of Virginia wine country with the coastal grit and culinary soul of Charm City, this Mid-Atlantic drive proves that the best itineraries are the ones that embrace contrast.

item.title: Where the Walls Talk
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
There is a distinct difference between visiting history and inhabiting it. Modern travel has long treated heritage as a spectator sport—a procession of roped-off museum rooms, plaque-reading in midday sun, and sanitized colonial revival lobbies that whisper nothing of the soil they stand upon. But a new vanguard of hoteliers and stewards is challenging this static approach.

To check into a true heritage property is to enter an ongoing story. It is the realization that the most profound luxury lies not in pristine, identical surfaces, but in the texture of memory: the cold weight of hand-carved limestone, the gentle creak of three-hundred-year-old timber, and the quiet dignity of spaces that have weathered empires, tides, and revolutions.

Part I: Stone, Fortresses & Coastal Rebirth

On an islet off the coast of Montenegro, guarding the entrance to the Bay of Kotor, sits Mamula Island. Built in the mid-19th century by Austro-Hungarian general Lazarus von Mamula, the circular stone fortress was engineered for siege and coastal defense—a towering ring of local masonry rising directly from the Adriatic. Today, as part of the broader heritage revitalization surrounding Luštica Bay, the fortress has undergone a delicate, high-design metamorphosis into an ultra-luxury sanctuary.

Rather than smoothing over its imposing architecture, the restoration honors the gravity of raw stone. Vaulted stone arches frame panoramic views of open water, light filters through former cannon ports, and minimalist interiors allow the weathered masonry to remain the main protagonist. The atmosphere is defined by dramatic maritime isolation. To sleep here is to feel the shelter of centuries-old ramparts while listening to salt spray strike the outer walls—a masterclass in how military architecture can be repurposed without losing its soul.

Farther west, across the Atlantic, a different architectural icon has confronted its own history. The British Colonial Nassau has stood along the Bahamian waterfront for over a century, long serving as a postcard emblem of 1920s grand hotel design. Yet its recent restoration represents something far more significant than a fresh coat of paint: a deliberate pivot from colonial nostalgia to authentic island ownership and cultural pride.

While preserving the stately proportions of its grand colonnades, high ceilings, and harbor views, the property has been reimagined to elevate contemporary Bahamian identity. Local artwork graces the walls, regional craftsmanship replaces generic imported decor, and the story told within its halls belongs firmly to the island’s people. It stands as a compelling model for heritage hospitality in the Caribbean—proving that iconic structures can honor their architectural roots while actively centering the culture of the community they inhabit.

Part II: Timber, Craft & Domestic Heritage

If stone evokes endurance, timber speaks to intimacy. On the quiet Caribbean island of Nevis, tucked beneath the shadow of a cloud-draped peak, lies The Hermitage. Built around a core structure dating back to the late 1600s, it is widely recognized as the oldest surviving wooden building in the region.

Constructed entirely of heavy lignum vitae hardwood using mortise-and-tenon joinery, the house has survived centuries of tropical storms and seismic shifts. Around it, gingerbread-trimmed cottages settle into lush botanical gardens. To step across the threshold is to enter a domestic lineage; floorboards settled over three centuries creak softly beneath barefoot travelers, and trade winds filter through wooden jalousie shutters just as they did in the 17th century. Hospitality here is intentionally unhurried and personal—feeling less like checking into a commercial resort and more like being welcomed onto a historic family estate.

Across the Atlantic, deep in the Scottish Highlands, history is preserved through texture and terroir. Sona’s Collection approaches heritage through material provenance, weaving clan history directly into the fabric of its estate lodgings.

Here, historic stone hearths crackle with local timber, and guest chambers are draped in custom hand-loomed tweeds and tartans sourced from regional mills. Every detail—from the curated single-malts reflecting the mineral profile of local springs to the estate stewardship that funds regional artisans—connects the traveler to the physical landscape. It is hospitality anchored in craft: an invitation to sit by an open fire, sip a dram with centuries of lineage, and look out over mist-laden glens from a space built to outlast generations.

The Art of the Steward-Hotelier

Properties like these remind us that the best travel experiences do not isolate us from a destination’s past—they ground us within it. Transforming a historic structure into a hotel requires a delicate balance: honoring original craft while forging a meaningful, modern purpose.

When you check out of a place where the walls talk, you carry away more than a souvenirs and photographs. You leave having participated in the living continuity of a place—a temporary guest in a building that will continue to tell its story long after you return home.

item.title: Don’t Miss the Top Features from The Story Continues Issue
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Over 40,000 readers have already explored the latest edition of Curated Travel Magazine, immersing themselves in stories that redefine how we see the world. As autumn unfolds, dive into the most popular features from The Story Continues issue before they slip into the archives.

From legendary rails and high-desert retreats to historic spa towns and vibrant spice markets, here are the top articles our readers loved most this season:

Heritage in Motion

Aboard Belmond’s Britannic Explorer, journey through Cornwall, Wales, and the Lake District, where rugged landscapes, living heritage, and regional traditions unfold right from the train window. From historic railways and slate quarries to farm-to-table cuisine by Simon Rogan, explore how Britain’s past continues to shape its modern luxury travel experience. Read it now: https://heyzine.com/flip-book/948d3f2612.html#page/10

Empire Crossroads

Explore the layered culinary history of Marrakech, where Amazigh traditions, Andalusian influences, and centuries of spice-route trade have shaped iconic dishes like tagine, pastilla, and tanjia. From the bustling ancient medina to the refined setting of Four Seasons Resort Marrakech, discover how food preserves the city’s history, culture, and enduring rituals of hospitality. Read it now: https://heyzine.com/flip-book/948d3f2612.html#page/14

Timeless Waters, Modern Revival

Discover Europe’s historic spa towns, where centuries-old thermal traditions meet the latest innovations in luxury wellness and preventative health. From Baden-Baden and Vichy to Karlovy Vary and Bath, see how mineral springs and grand bathing heritage are being reimagined through modern longevity treatments, recovery therapies, and digital detoxes. Read it now: https://heyzine.com/flip-book/948d3f2612.html#page/36

Rails into the Wild

Travel deep into landscapes largely untouched by roads aboard two extraordinary rail journeys: Canada’s Hudson Bay Line to the subarctic wilderness of Churchill, and Switzerland’s Glacier and Bernina Express through the high Alps. From beluga whales and polar bears to dramatic glaciers and alpine villages, learn how the train transforms remote transit into an immersive encounter with the wild. Read it now: https://heyzine.com/flip-book/948d3f2612.html#page/46

The Mother Road, Redefined

Reimagine Route 66 through three curated lenses—wellness, architecture, and food—rather than attempting the traditional 2,400-mile road trip in one sweep. From high-desert mineral springs and Midwestern design landmarks to heritage ranches and Southwestern farm-to-table cuisine, discover how slowing down and choosing depth over distance creates a truly meaningful luxury journey. Read it now: https://heyzine.com/flip-book/948d3f2612.html#page/49

item.title: Coral Reefs and Rainforest Discovery on Malaysia’s Gaya Island
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Just four degrees north of the equator, Gaya Island offers a tropical retreat within Malaysia’s Tunku Abdul Rahman Marine Park, where rainforest, coral reefs, and rich biodiversity create opportunities for discovery on land and underwater. At Gaya Island Resort, guests can learn about reef conservation at the resort’s Marine Center, join guided nature walks, or explore the surrounding waters through snorkeling and diving excursions. The resort’s PURE programming introduces guests to the island’s natural environment and cultural heritage, while Spa Village offers nature-inspired treatments for a more restorative interlude. For travelers escaping colder climates, the island provides more than a change in temperature: it offers a chance to understand the ecosystems and cultural traditions that make this corner of Borneo distinctive.

The Curated Take

Gaya Island’s appeal lies in the close relationship between forest, sea, and local heritage. Travelers can move from guided walks through the island’s natural environment to coral reef exploration, with conservation learning adding context to the experience. It is an appealing choice for those who want a warm-weather retreat that pairs relaxation with a deeper appreciation of the destination.

item.title: A Nature-Led Island Escape in the Maldives
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
In the North Malé Atoll, Baros Maldives offers a warm-weather retreat where turquoise waters, coral reefs, and Indian Ocean sunsets set the pace. Just a short speedboat journey from Malé Airport, the island combines intimate surroundings with opportunities to discover the marine environment that defines the Maldives. Guests can snorkel among vibrant coral formations, explore underwater landscapes on diving excursions, or watch the light change across the ocean from a private deck. Environmental awareness is also part of the experience, with educational programs and excursions to uninhabited islands helping guests understand the importance of protecting the region’s ecosystems. For travelers trading winter cold for tropical sunshine, Baros offers both the pleasures of island living and opportunities to connect with the natural world.

The Curated Take

The Maldives is often imagined as a place to retreat from the world, but its reefs and island ecosystems are an essential part of the experience. At Baros, time on the water can become an introduction to the marine environment, while conservation-focused activities offer a reason to look beyond the postcard views. For travelers seeking warmth with a greater sense of connection to place, this is an island escape with substance beneath the surface.

item.title: Winter Sunshine and Dutch-Caribbean Culture on Aruba’s Palm Beach
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers ready to trade winter coats for turquoise water and warm Caribbean breezes, Aruba offers a sunny escape with plenty to discover beyond the shoreline. On the island’s celebrated Palm Beach, Aruba Marriott Resort & Stellaris Casino combines beachfront relaxation with culinary experiences, wellness amenities, and access to Aruba’s distinctive Dutch-Caribbean culture. Recent enhancements include refreshed guestrooms and an updated adults-only H2Oasis pool, with four private plunge pools set to debut in select accommodations within the adults-only Tradewinds experience in December 2026. Guests can savor Dutch-inspired pancakes at Nana’s or enjoy fresh seafood at Atardi, where dinner comes with views of the setting sun over the Caribbean. Beyond the resort, Aruba’s contrasting landscapes invite exploration, from the rugged terrain of Arikok National Park to the colorful art scene of San Nicolas and the island’s snorkeling and sailing waters.

The Curated Take

Aruba’s appeal lies in the contrast between its easygoing beach life and the distinctive landscapes and cultural influences that make the island more than a sun-and-sand destination. Palm Beach offers a relaxed starting point, while inland adventures and the art of San Nicolas reveal another side of the island. For winter travelers seeking reliable warmth, a comfortable beachfront base, and opportunities to explore at their own pace, Aruba makes a compelling case for a Caribbean reset.

item.title: A New Caribbean Beachfront Escape on Grenada’s Scenic Coast
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Grenada is welcoming a new luxury retreat to its picturesque coastline with the debut of InterContinental Grenada Resort & Spa, expected in November 2026. The beachfront property will feature 120 rooms and suites, a Beach Club, multiple dining venues, and a dedicated spa, offering travelers a fresh setting for a winter escape in the Caribbean. With its combination of coastal scenery, opportunities for relaxation, and the comforts of a full-service resort, the new arrival adds another option for travelers seeking warm weather and a change of pace during the colder months.

The Curated Take

For travelers who have explored the Caribbean’s familiar luxury destinations, a new resort can offer a reason to look somewhere different. Grenada’s scenic coastline provides the backdrop for this forthcoming beachfront retreat, where dining, spa experiences, and time by the sea promise a restorative winter getaway. Its debut also offers an opportunity to discover more of the island beyond the traditional Caribbean beach escape.

item.title: Sunlit Days and Castaway Nights in the Maldives’ Baa Atoll
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
In the Baa Atoll UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, Milaidhoo Maldives offers a boutique island escape surrounded by warm waters and remarkable marine life. The Maldives’ drier season, from January through April, brings particularly appealing conditions for days spent outdoors. Guests can explore the house reef with the resort’s resident marine biologist, looking for green turtles, spotted eagle rays, and reef sharks, or head out on a traditional dhoni at sunset in search of dolphins and whale sharks. For a more secluded experience, an overnight stay on a private sandbank offers the chance to spend the night beneath the stars, surrounded by the Indian Ocean. During the festive period, the resort’s A Tropical Season of Joy program adds beachside yoga, sound meditation, breathwork, Maldivian cultural performances, and a Spice Route-inspired dinner celebrating culinary traditions from across the country’s 26 atolls.

The Curated Take

Milaidhoo offers a particularly evocative version of the Maldivian escape: intimate, nature-focused, and shaped by experiences that extend beyond the villa. Exploring the reef with a marine biologist brings insight to the surrounding waters, while a night on a private sandbank transforms the familiar luxury of an island stay into something more elemental. For travelers seeking winter sunshine with a sense of wonder, the combination of marine discovery, cultural depth, and starlit solitude is especially compelling.
